title: Nehemiah 7:39–60
context: The list continues with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon’s servants, paralleling Ezra 2:36-58. The priestly figures match Ezra exactly, while the singers and gatekeepers differ slightly, and several temple-servant names are spelled differently, with three names in Ezra 2 not appearing here. The small number of Levites, compared with thousands of priests, stands out in both lists.

verses.text: The priests: The children of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua: nine hundred seventy-three.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, number nine hundred seventy-three, as in Ezra 2:36. Arminian readers see the priestly line surviving exile and ready to serve again at the altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jedaiah is the second priestly course in 1 Chronicles 24:7. All four priestly figures in this section agree with Ezra to the last digit.

verses.text: The children of Immer: one thousand fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Immer’s priests number one thousand fifty-two, as in Ezra 2:37. Arminian readers note how large the priestly families are compared with the Levites listed shortly after.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Immer is the sixteenth course in David’s arrangement (1 Chronicles 24:14). Careful preservation of these lines reflects concern for legitimate service at the altar.

verses.text: The children of Pashhur: one thousand two hundred forty-seven.
verses.arminianNotes: The children of Pashhur: one thousand two hundred forty-seven, matching Ezra 2:38. Arminian readers note that this is the largest priestly family in the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Pashhur does not appear among the twenty-four courses of 1 Chronicles 24, though a Pashhur appears in the priestly genealogy of 1 Chronicles 9:12. How the family relates to the courses is discussed by interpreters.

verses.text: The children of Harim: one thousand seventeen.
verses.arminianNotes: The priestly Harim numbers one thousand seventeen, as in Ezra 2:39. Arminian readers add up the four priestly families and find four thousand two hundred eighty-nine priests in all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Harim is the third course in 1 Chronicles 24:8. The priests make up roughly a tenth of the stated total, a striking proportion for one tribe’s servants.

verses.text: The Levites: the children of Jeshua, of Kadmiel, of the children of Hodevah: seventy-four.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel: seventy-four, matching Ezra 2:40, though Ezra spells the ancestor Hodaviah. Arminian readers note how few Levites returned compared with the priests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the shortage of Levites continued; Ezra later found none among his company and had to send for them (Ezra 8:15-20). The small number is noted in both lists.

verses.text: The singers: the children of Asaph: one hundred forty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: The singers: the children of Asaph: one hundred forty-eight, where Ezra 2:41 has one hundred twenty-eight. Arminian readers see the singers returning to restore the praise of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Asaph’s family had been appointed by David over temple music (1 Chronicles 25:1). The difference in number is named without resolution.

verses.text: The gatekeepers: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai: one hundred thirty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: The gatekeepers, six families: one hundred thirty-eight, where Ezra 2:42 has one hundred thirty-nine. Arminian readers note that the gatekeepers’ service, though humble, was essential to the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Shallum, Talmon, and Akkub appear as gatekeeper families in 1 Chronicles 9:17. The difference of one is named here without any attempt at resolution.

verses.text: The temple servants: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth,
verses.arminianNotes: The temple servants begin with Ziha, Hasupha, and Tabbaoth, as in Ezra 2:43. Arminian readers see those assigned to lowly service listed by name alongside priests and nobles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ezra 8:20 traces the temple servants to David’s appointment to assist the Levites. Their inclusion shows that every role in God’s house mattered.

verses.text: the children of Keros, the children of Sia, the children of Padon,
verses.arminianNotes: Keros, Sia, and Padon follow. Ezra 2:44 reads Siaha for the second name, one of several small spelling differences in this part of the record. Arminian readers note each variant briefly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the families of temple servants preserved in both lists despite their modest status. God’s record includes the humblest servants of his house.

verses.text: the children of Lebana, the children of Hagaba, the children of Salmai,
verses.arminianNotes: Lebana, Hagaba, and Salmai appear here. Ezra 2:45-46 has Lebanah, Hagabah, Akkub, Hagab, and Shamlai, so two names in Ezra have no counterpart in this verse. Arminian readers record the difference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers count this among the larger name variations between the lists. Salmai and Shamlai look like forms of one name, while Akkub and Hagab are simply absent here.

verses.text: the children of Hanan, the children of Giddel, the children of Gahar,
verses.arminianNotes: Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar agree with Ezra 2:46-47. Arminian readers see families who worked in the background of temple life returning to take up their duties again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the agreement of these names in both books shows the shared record behind the lists. Even minor families are carefully preserved.

verses.text: the children of Reaiah, the children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda,
verses.arminianNotes: Reaiah, Rezin, and Nekoda agree with Ezra 2:47-48. Arminian readers notice that Nekoda appears again in verse 62 among the families unable to prove their descent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers suggest the repeated name may belong to different families. The record carefully separates those with a recorded lineage from those who lacked one.

verses.text: the children of Gazzam, the children of Uzza, the children of Paseah,
verses.arminianNotes: Gazzam, Uzza, and Paseah agree with Ezra 2:48-49. Arminian readers see the record moving steadily on, giving each family its line without distinction of rank or wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a Joiada son of Paseah repaired the Old Gate (Nehemiah 3:6), though whether he belonged to this family of temple servants is uncertain.

verses.text: the children of Besai, the children of Meunim, the children of Nephushesim,
verses.arminianNotes: Besai, Meunim, and Nephushesim follow. Ezra 2:49-50 includes Asnah, which is missing here, and spells the last name Nephisim. Arminian readers record both differences without comment on cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers suggest the name Meunim may point to a foreign origin, perhaps related to the Meunites of 2 Chronicles 26:7, though this is uncertain. Outsiders may have been absorbed into temple service.

verses.text: the children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur,
verses.arminianNotes: Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harhur agree with Ezra 2:51. Arminian readers see these families as part of the full community that returned to rebuild worship in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that these temple servants are remembered by name even though nothing more is known of most of them. A place in the record is itself a kind of honor.

verses.text: the children of Bazlith, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha,
verses.arminianNotes: Bazlith, Mehida, and Harsha follow; Ezra 2:52 has Bazluth for the first. Arminian readers treat such spelling variants as natural in lists handed down separately over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that differences of a vowel or letter are common in parallel lists. They do not change which family is meant but show the records were transmitted independently.

verses.text: the children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Temah,
verses.arminianNotes: Barkos, Sisera, and Temah agree with Ezra 2:53. Arminian readers note that the name Sisera recalls the Canaanite commander of Judges 4, though no connection is stated or implied.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that some temple-servant names may reflect non-Israelite origins, though the text gives no explanation. All are now part of the returning community.

verses.text: the children of Neziah, and the children of Hatipha.
verses.arminianNotes: Neziah and Hatipha close the temple servants, as in Ezra 2:54. Arminian readers see the completion of a record that honors every family that made the journey home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers count thirty-two temple-servant families in Nehemiah 7:46-56, against thirty-five in Ezra 2:43-54. The combined total for this group and Solomon’s servants follows in verse 60.

verses.text: The children of Solomon’s servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Perida,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon’s servants begin with Sotai, Sophereth, and Perida. Ezra 2:55 reads Hassophereth and Peruda, small spelling differences. Arminian readers see another humble group counted among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers suggest Solomon’s servants may descend from those Solomon conscripted for labor (1 Kings 9:20-21), though the origin of the group is not stated. They too return to serve.

verses.text: the children of Jaala, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel,
verses.arminianNotes: Jaala, Darkon, and Giddel follow, with Ezra 2:56 spelling the first Jaalah. Arminian readers see even the smallest households of servants given their place in the record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the name Giddel also appears among the temple servants in verse 49. The repetition may reflect different families sharing a name.

verses.text: the children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth Hazzebaim, and the children of Amon.
verses.arminianNotes: Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Amon close this group. Ezra 2:57 ends with Ami instead of Amon. Arminian readers note that both lists count ten families of Solomon’s servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the name Shephatiah also appears among the lay families in verse 9. The list of Solomon’s servants closes with these names before the combined total.

verses.text: All the temple servants and the children of Solomon’s servants were three hundred ninety-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Temple servants and Solomon’s servants together number three hundred ninety-two, matching Ezra 2:58. Arminian readers find it notable that the sum agrees even where individual names vary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared total as a sign that both lists draw on one underlying record. The humble servants are counted as part of God’s people alongside priests and nobles.
